subject: Accounting
title: Why Cash Flow Matters
description: Learn Why Cash Flow Matters in one minute.

hook.text: A company reports $5 million profit but can't pay its employees. How? Profit isn't cash.

buildup.text: The income statement shows profit. The cash flow statement shows actual money movement.

discovery.text: Revenue recorded on credit boosts profit but delivers zero cash until the customer pays.

twist.text: Many profitable companies have gone bankrupt simply because they ran out of cash.

climax.text: Experienced investors always check cash flow—it's harder to fake than net income.

punchline.text: Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact.

quiz.question: Why can a profitable company go bankrupt?
options: It runs out of actual cash

details.summary: The cash flow statement tracks actual cash moving in and out of a business, revealing whether the company can fund its operations, invest in growth, and return money to shareholders. This topic explains why cash flow matters more than profit for survival.
details.whyItMatters: Companies don't go bankrupt from lack of profit—they go bankrupt from lack of cash. The cash flow statement reveals the ultimate truth about a company's financial viability.
takeaways: The cash flow statement has three sections: operating, investing, and financing activities
A profitable company can still run out of cash if receivables aren't collected or inventory ties up capital
Free cash flow (operating minus capex) is the money truly available for distribution or reinvestment

faq.question: Why is cash flow more important than profit?
faq.answer: Profit is an accounting concept that includes non-cash items and estimates. Cash flow shows actual money in the bank. A company can be profitable on paper while running out of cash—because revenue was recorded before collection, or capital was tied up in inventory.

faq.question: What are the three sections of the cash flow statement?
faq.answer: Operating activities (cash from core business operations), investing activities (cash spent on or received from long-term assets), and financing activities (cash from or returned to capital providers). Together, they reconcile the beginning and ending cash balance.
